edges.relationship: Joins interpretive understanding of meaningful social action with a requirement for causal adequacy.
edges.evidence_note: Own methodological excerpt, Definition and §7 read; intelligibility alone does not establish a causal account. Excerpt-based contribution, without adopting historical racial/animal asides.

edges.relationship: Explains how value-relevant selection identifies a historical problem while causal explanation still requires evidence.
edges.evidence_note: Own Objectivity excerpt’s cultural-significance/value-relevance paragraphs read; the theoretical resource concerns selection and explanation, not an assertion that all comparative sociology follows Weber.

edges.relationship: Distinguishes recollective recognition from the critical comparison of testimonies and documents in historical knowledge.
edges.evidence_note: Own dialogue, PDF pp. 4–5, passage from recognition to the archive; testimony is fallible and can be criticized. Personal forgiveness is explicitly distinguished from state amnesty and judicial impunity in PDF pp. 1–3. Book body unread.

edges.relationship: Uses movement between historical scales to think about determination, uncertainty and actors’ limited horizons.
edges.evidence_note: Own dialogue, PDF pp. 5–7, discussions of Revel, Braudel and Menocchio. This is an epistemological resource attributed to Ricoeur, not a claim that he practised or founded microhistory, or independent verification of his account of other historians.

edges.relationship: Makes production relations, productive forces and the forms in which people fight conflicts central historical questions.
edges.evidence_note: Own 1859 preface core paragraphs read. Strong forces/relations propositions are Marx’s argument; the existing separately sourced 1877 rejection of a universal Western-European path remains in the group context.

edges.relationship: Criticizes colonial land restriction as a means of making people dependent on wage labour.
edges.evidence_note: Own Capital I chapter 33 opening and colonial-land discussion read. This is a specific criticism of Wakefield; Mill is not named in this passage, and no direct Marx-to-Mill attack or complete Indigenous history is inferred.

edges.relationship: Analyzes how institutional production and unequal social positions allow differently coded readings of media.
edges.evidence_note: Own 1973 paper pp. 1–3 and 16–18 read; encoding and decoding are distinct determinate moments. The early paper’s professional-code position and the later revision remain distinct.

edges.relationship: Treats diasporic identity as historically produced positioning, transformation and difference, alongside the political force of recovery.
edges.evidence_note: Own essay pp. 222–226 read in the qualified scan witness. Hall recognizes the resistance value of recovery while rejecting an eternally unchanged essence; no identity-history founding claim follows.

edges.relationship: Challenges homogeneous progressive time and the inheritance of culture through the victors of history.
edges.evidence_note: Own theses VI–IX and XIII–XIV read; this is a contribution associated with Frankfurt critical inquiry, not institutional membership or a single Frankfurt doctrine.

edges.relationship: Makes remembrance of silenced and oppressed predecessors a demand on historical representation.
edges.evidence_note: Own theses II–III, VI and XII read. A conceptual resource, not a title-based claim of influence on every later memory historian; separate specific reception evidence remains unchanged.

edges.relationship: Treats social space as produced through practices and power, beyond inventories or textual decoding alone.
edges.evidence_note: Own 1974 introduction excerpt, pp. 19–20 reread; conceptual resource for spatial history, with historical reconstruction and GIS kept distinct.

edges.relationship: Examines space as an active medium in the conflicting operations of capital and class hegemony.
edges.evidence_note: Own excerpt, pp. 21–22 reread: distinguishes forms of capital and refuses to make capitalism a closed, contradiction-free system. This is Lefebvre’s theoretical intervention, not a verified general law of capitalist history.

edges.relationship: Joins culture as ordinary social meanings and ways of life with artistic learning and creative work.
edges.evidence_note: Own Culture Is Ordinary, pp. 92–94 read; the essay’s conjunction is preserved instead of reducing culture either to elite arts or to an undifferentiated way of life.

edges.relationship: Criticizes a prescriptive Marxist account that would dictate cultural meanings and artistic forms from a proposed system of production.
edges.evidence_note: Own essay pp. 95–96 read. He retains the importance of production and restricted educational access while rejecting directive cultural prescriptions; this is criticism within his engagement with Marxism, not rejection of all materialist historical analysis.

edges.relationship: Studies situated encounters through participants’ attempts to establish and manage a definition of the situation.
edges.evidence_note: Own introduction pp. 1–4 read; social inference and interactional responses are the object, not evidence that he founded practice-oriented historiography.

edges.relationship: Distinguishes intentionally given expressions from impressions others infer from expressions given off.
edges.evidence_note: Own introduction pp. 1–5 read. A specific resource for examining socially performed identities; not a claim of direct influence on all identity histories or an equation of tactical self-presentation with all diasporic identity formation.
